summary.text: Surface currents are ocean currents driven mainly by wind systems, with the Coriolis effect playing a major role in how they develop.
Because of the Ekman spiral they flow at an angle to the winds that drive them, turning clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and counter-clockwise in the Southern.
Warm currents raise temperatures along the coasts they pass, and the Gulf Stream with the North Atlantic Drift makes northwest Europe more temperate than other places that far north.

items.prompt: A floating bottle is carried hundreds of kilometres across the sea surface by a current. What mainly powers that current?

options.label: Differences in salt and temperature
Heat from undersea volcanoes
Rivers pouring into the ocean
Winds blowing over the ocean

items.explain: Surface currents are generally driven by wind systems; differences in temperature and salinity mainly drive deep-water currents.

items.prompt: A steady wind blows across the sea in the Northern Hemisphere. How does the surface water it drives tend to move?

options.label: At an angle, spiralling clockwise
Straight in the wind's direction
Straight against the wind
Downward toward the seabed

items.explain: The Ekman spiral makes currents flow at an angle to the driving winds, with clockwise spirals in the Northern Hemisphere.

items.prompt: Lima, Peru, sits among tropical latitudes yet has a cooler climate than its surroundings. What explains this?

options.label: Its spot far inland from any sea
A cool ocean current flowing offshore
Ash clouds from nearby volcanoes
Winds blowing straight from the Arctic

items.explain: Lima's cooler subtropical climate stands out from its tropical surroundings because of the Humboldt Current.

items.prompt: A warm current runs along a coast. How does it raise the temperature of the town on shore?

options.label: It heats the rocks under the town
It raises sea level into warm floods
It clears away clouds above the coast
It warms the sea breezes that blow inland

items.explain: Warm currents along temperate coasts raise local temperatures by warming the sea breezes that blow over them.

items.prompt: An oceanographer says a current carries 30 sverdrups. What is being measured?

options.label: The volume of water flowing each second
The speed of the water in km per hour
The temperature of the water
The amount of salt in the water

items.explain: A sverdrup is a volume flow rate: 1 Sv equals 1,000,000 cubic metres of water per second.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning about Europe's climate is wrong. Which?

steps.text: Northwest Europe lies at a high latitude.
Ocean currents move water but leave the temperature of nearby land unchanged.
The Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift flow toward northwest Europe.
So northwest Europe should be as cold as other places that far north.

beats.explain: Currents do change land temperatures: warm currents warm the sea breezes that blow ashore, which is why the Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift make northwest Europe more temperate for its latitude.

beats.idea: Winds, bent by the Coriolis effect, drive surface currents that carry warmth or coolness to the coasts they pass.

paragraphs.heading: Water on the move
paragraphs.text: An ocean current is a steady flow of seawater in one direction. Several forces set it going, including wind, the Coriolis effect, breaking waves, and differences in temperature and salt. Currents come in two basic kinds: surface currents and deep-water currents. Surface currents are mostly pushed by wind, while deep currents are driven by differences in how dense the water is.

paragraphs.heading: Driven by the wind
paragraphs.text: Big prevailing winds drive the major long-lasting currents. Seasonal or occasional winds drive currents that last only as long as those winds do. The Coriolis effect plays a major part in how these currents develop. Because of a pattern called the Ekman spiral, the water ends up flowing at an angle to the wind, curving clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and counter-clockwise in the Southern. Surface currents also shift a little with the seasons, most clearly near the equator.

paragraphs.heading: Narrow in the west, broad in the east
paragraphs.text: Surface currents in deep ocean basins are lopsided. The branch on the east side, flowing toward the equator, is wide and spread out. The branch on the west side, flowing toward the pole, is fairly narrow and is called a western boundary current. The shape of the sea floor, the outline of the coast and meetings with other currents all affect where a current goes and how strong it is.

paragraphs.heading: Drifts, currents and streams
paragraphs.text: Currents are sorted by temperature into warm and cold ones. They are also sorted by speed, size and direction. A drift, such as the North Atlantic Drift, is surface water pushed forward by the prevailing wind. A current, such as the Labrador Current, moves faster and in a clearer direction, and a stream, such as the Gulf Stream, carries bigger masses of water faster still. Flow is measured in sverdrups, where 1 Sv equals 1,000,000 m³ of water passing each second.

paragraphs.heading: Carrying warmth and cold
paragraphs.text: Currents change the temperature of the places they pass. A warm current running along a temperate coast warms the sea breezes that blow over it, and so warms the land. The Gulf Stream and its extension, the North Atlantic Drift, make northwest Europe much milder than other places that far north. Another case is Lima, Peru, where the Humboldt Current brings a cooler climate than the tropical lands around it.

paragraphs.heading: The biggest current and the deep link
paragraphs.text: The largest current of all is the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, which the wind drives clockwise around Antarctica without a break. It joins all the ocean basins together. Surface flows also feed the deep ocean. Wind-driven currents like the Gulf Stream travel toward the pole from the equatorial Atlantic, cool on the way, and finally sink at high latitudes to form North Atlantic Deep Water, which then spreads into the ocean basins.
